The Problem

The UserManagement service manages three entities: User, Roles, Permissions. Each entity supports five operations: create, get, update, delete, list. That is fifteen handler methods.

Each handler method follows the same structure:

  1. Start an OTEL span.

  2. Unmarshal the incoming NATS message body into a typed event struct.

  3. Run all pre-hooks for this operation, in priority order, distinguishing sync (can abort) from async (fire-and-forget).

  4. Validate required fields.

  5. Set span attributes.

  6. Forward the request to the DAL via NATS request-reply with a 30-second timeout.

  7. Run all post-hooks, distinguishing sync (transforms the response) from async (fire-and-forget).

  8. Reply to the original NATS message.

That is eight steps, repeated fifteen times across three files. On top of that, two relations (UserRoles, RolesPermissions) add six more handler methods with a similar but distinct structure.

Twenty-one handler methods total. The structure is identical across all of them except for the type names and subject strings.

The Scale of the Boilerplate

The UserManagement service requires, per entity:

Artifact Lines Content

Handler code

~595

CRUD operations, hook dispatch, validation

SQL schema

8

Table definition with constraints

Hook stubs

30+

4 signatures × multiple operations

Integration tests

21

End-to-end pipeline validation

For three entities (User, Roles, Permissions): 1,790 lines of Go.

A developer adding a fourth entity — say, Tenants — must write another 400+ lines of Go following this recipe exactly. Miss step 3 and pre-hooks silently do not run. Miss step 7 and post-hooks silently do not run. Get the DAL subject string wrong and the service appears to work until a specific operation triggers a silent routing failure.

The structure is a recipe. The problem is that the recipe is held in a developer’s head rather than written down in a form a machine can execute.

The Recipe Analogy

A professional kitchen does not rely on every chef memorizing the same recipes. It writes them down. Consistency comes from the recipe, not from the chef’s memory.

The equivalent in software is a template. When every entity handler follows the exact same structure — unmarshal, pre-hooks, validate, DAL forward, post-hooks, respond — that structure is a recipe. The specific entity (User, Roles, Permissions) is an ingredient list.

Hand-writing 1,790 lines of Go from a mental recipe carries specific failure modes:

  • Mistakes that a text editor cannot catch (wrong subject string, missing hook call, copy-paste with the wrong type name).

  • Every new entity means another ~400 lines of hand-written boilerplate.

  • When the recipe changes — OTEL span attributes need to appear in a new place — every handler must be updated by hand.

The recipe should be written down once, in a form a computer can execute.

What a Solution Looks Like

The right solution separates what an entity is from how a handler works.

A developer declares:

Entity: User
  fields: id (uuid, primaryKey), username (string), email (email), password (password, hidden)
  operations: create, get, update, delete, list
  hooks on create: preCreateD (pre-sync), preCreateM (pre-async), postCreateNotifyAdmin (post-async)

A code generator reads this declaration and produces the 400-line handler file, correctly, every time. The developer never touches the generated file. When the recipe changes, the generator changes — and all handlers regenerate correctly.

This is what the UserManagement DSL does. The MPS projectional editor holds the declaration. TextGen templates encode the recipe. sync.sh runs the pipeline. The result is 1,790 lines of correct, consistent Go code that no developer hand-writes or hand-maintains.

Design rationale: The DSL does not generate all Go code. It generates the structural scaffolding — the handler skeletons, the event types, the NATS wiring. Business logic lives in userDefinedHooks.go, which is preserved across regeneration by merge_hooks.py. The split is intentional: generated code should be disposable; business logic should not be.

The Question This Answers

What if adding a new entity required 15 lines of DSL instead of 300 lines of Go?

The answer is yes — with the UserManagement DSL, adding a fourth entity is approximately 15 lines of DSL declaration. The generator produces the handler file. No hand-writing. No missed steps.

The rest of this guide explains how the system achieves this, what constraints shape its architecture, and where the failure modes live.

Watch for:

  • The urge to "just hand-write it this one time." It is always this one time until it is the fifteenth time.

  • Generated code that is also manually edited. When the generator reruns, edits disappear. If you find yourself editing generated files, the right fix is to change the template or add a hook.

  • Boilerplate growth that scales with entity count. If adding a new entity requires changes in N places proportional to the entity’s operation count, the recipe exists but has no recipe book.

The Big Picture

The UserManagement service is a business logic layer. It sits between callers and a Data Access Layer (DAL), adding validation, hooks, and OTEL tracing to every operation. It does not store data — it processes requests and forwards them.

Understanding this positioning is the key to understanding every architectural decision that follows.

The Postal Service Analogy

Think of the system as a postal network.

NATS subjects are street addresses. motadata.user.create is as specific as "123 Main Street." Any message sent to that address lands in exactly one mailbox — the User entity handler’s HandleCreate method.

The handler is the mailbox. It receives the letter (incoming NATS message), checks it for completeness (validation), stamps it with business context (OTEL span attributes, hook results), and re-routes it to the warehouse address (the DAL subject motadata.user.db.create).

The DAL is the warehouse. It stores and retrieves the actual goods. The UserManagement service is the post office — it does not store anything, it processes and routes.

In this analogy, `demo.sh’s mock DAL responders are a warehouse simulator: they accept any delivery and reply "received" without actually storing anything. This lets the entire postal network — addressing, routing, validation, hooks — be tested without a real warehouse.

The Two Flows

There are two distinct flows to understand: the generation flow (how the code comes to exist) and the runtime flow (what happens when a message arrives).

Generation Flow

MPS DSL (UserManagmentMps/)
  │
  │  TextGen templates run in MPS
  │
  ▼
source_gen/*.go  (MPS output)
  │
  │  sync.sh
  │    1. Copy .go/.sql to src/
  │    2. merge_hooks.py (extract hook stubs, preserve implementations)
  │    3. Extract project name from main.go first-line comment
  │    4. rsync SDK from ~/projects/nextgen/gosdk/
  │    5. Patch SDK module path (motadatagosdk → dev.azure.com/...)
  │    6. Fix SDK internal imports
  │    7. Kill processes on ports 4229/8222
  │    8. docker compose build && up
  │
  ▼
Running Docker container (NATS microservice)

The DSL is the single source of truth. Every file in src/ except userDefinedHooks.go is generated — it will be overwritten the next time MPS regenerates and sync.sh runs. The only file safe to edit by hand is userDefinedHooks.go.

Runtime Flow

1. Client publishes: nats req motadata.user.create '{"username":"alice","email":"alice@co.com",...}'

2. main.go routes to User handler's HandleCreate method

3. HandleCreate:
   a. Start OTEL span "user.create"
   b. Unmarshal body → UserCreatedEvent
   c. Pre-hooks (sorted by priority):
        preCreateD (sync) → validate or abort
        preCreateM (async) → fire notification, continue
   d. Validate required fields (returns error if missing)
   e. Set span attributes (user.username, user.email, ...)
   f. NATS request → motadata.user.db.create (30s timeout)
   g. Post-hooks:
        postCreateNotifyAdmin (async) → fire admin alert
   h. Reply to original request with DAL response

4. DAL processes motadata.user.db.create and replies

5. Client receives response

Design rationale: The subject split — motadata.user.create for incoming, motadata.user.db.create for DAL — is not accidental. It means the UserManagement service can be inserted between any caller and any DAL without callers or the DAL needing to change their subject patterns. The business layer is a middleware that speaks both languages.

Component Responsibilities

Component Responsibility

MPS DSL (UserManagmentMps/)

Single source of truth. Defines entities, fields, operations, relations, hooks, and the NatsServer configuration.

TextGen templates

Encode the handler recipe. Produce user.go, roles.go, permissions.go, main.go, and sqlPrem_init_sql.sql from DSL declarations.

merge_hooks.py

Extracts hook stubs from generated entity files, merges them into userDefinedHooks.go, and detects signature changes. Preserves user implementations across regeneration.

sync.sh

Orchestrates the full pipeline: copy from MPS, run merge, vendor+patch SDK, kill old containers, rebuild and restart.

userDefinedHooks.go

The only file safe to edit. Contains all business logic as hook implementations. Preserved across regeneration.

Docker Compose

Runs NATS (port 4229 external, 4222 internal) + the app container. The app connects to NATS at nats://nats:4222 on the internal network.

demo.sh

21 end-to-end tests. Spawns mock DAL responders, sends nats req messages, verifies responses.

The Subject Hierarchy

Every NATS subject in the system follows two patterns:

Incoming (business layer): motadata.{entity}.{operation}

Examples: motadata.user.create, motadata.roles.list, motadata.user.roles.assign

Outgoing (DAL): motadata.{entity}.db.{operation}

Examples: motadata.user.db.create, motadata.roles.db.list

For relations, the pattern extends: motadata.{from}.{to}.db.{operation}

This hierarchy is not configured anywhere — it is generated by TextGen from the entity and relation names in the DSL. Change an entity name in MPS and the subject strings change everywhere automatically.

The NATS Micro Bridge

main.go uses the nats.go/micro package to expose the service over NATS’s microservice protocol. This gives the service:

  • Automatic service discovery via $SRV.INFO

  • Structured endpoint registration per operation

  • A standard way to inspect what subjects the service handles

The service name comes from the first-line comment in the generated main.go:

// MotaDSLUM
package main

sync.sh extracts this comment with head -1 src/main.go | sed 's|^// *||' and passes it as a Docker build argument. Single source of truth: the DSL’s NatsServer concept generates the comment, and everything downstream (Dockerfile, container name) derives from it.

Design rationale: Using a first-line comment as the service name source is pragmatic, not elegant. A config file would be cleaner, but the comment is generated automatically from the DSL’s NatsServer concept — no manual configuration required. The generator writes it; the pipeline reads it.

What the System Does Not Do

Understanding system boundaries prevents surprises:

  • No persistence. The UserManagement service does not connect to a database. All reads and writes go through the DAL.

  • No authentication. Auth is handled upstream. The service assumes messages arrive from trusted callers.

  • No retry logic. NATS request-reply uses a 30-second timeout. If the DAL does not respond, the call fails. No retry.

  • No schema migrations. The generated sqlPrem_init_sql.sql creates the initial schema. Migrations are out of scope.

Watch for:

  • Editing files in src/ that are not userDefinedHooks.go. They will be overwritten on the next sync.sh run.

  • Hardcoded subject strings in hook implementations. If the entity name changes, generated subjects change but hardcoded strings in hooks do not.

  • Missing mock DAL responders in test scripts. If demo.sh does not spawn a responder for a subject, tests for that entity will time out rather than fail with a clear error.

The DSL

Why Not Just Write Go?

The structural problem with hand-writing entity handlers is not the typing — it is the mental model that must be held simultaneously: "in HandleCreate, step 3 is pre-hooks sorted by priority, step 4 is validation, step 5 is span attributes."

Miss step 3 and pre-hooks silently do not fire. Get the order wrong and the validator runs before hooks can abort, which means aborted requests still reach the DAL.

The failure mode has a name: maintaining consistency through discipline. It fails as the codebase grows because humans make mistakes under repetition.

The right approach is to encode the recipe once, in a form a machine can execute reliably. That form is a DSL.

Three Pillars of the DSL Approach

Consistency. Every handler follows the exact same eight-step structure because they are all produced by the same template. It is not possible to accidentally skip step 3 in roles.go but not user.go — the template either generates it everywhere or nowhere.

Single source of truth. The entity name User appears in the Go struct, the event types (UserCreatedEvent, UserGetRequest), the NATS subjects (motadata.user.create), the SQL table name (iam.user), and the span attributes (user.username). In hand-written code, these are four separate places to update. In the DSL, they derive from one declaration.

Generation velocity. Adding a fourth entity (say, Tenants) requires writing ~15 lines of DSL. The generator produces the handler file. No hand-writing. No missed steps.

Trade-offs honestly stated: The DSL approach costs something real. Learning MPS is a non-trivial investment with a steep initial curve. The TextGen templates must be maintained — a bug in the template affects all generated files simultaneously. And debugging generated code requires tracing backward from the output to the template node that produced it, without line numbers or breakpoints.

These are real costs. The system is worth it when the entity count is growing and consistency matters more than flexibility. It is not worth it for a one-off handler.

MPS for Go Developers

MPS is a projectional editor, not a text editor. This is the most important thing to understand before anything else.

In a text editor, you write characters and the parser turns them into a syntax tree. In MPS, you directly edit the syntax tree — the tree is the document. There are no characters in between.

The analogy: a spreadsheet versus a word processor. In a word processor, you type "=SUM(A1:A10)" and the parser interprets it. In a spreadsheet, you click a cell, click a function button, and the spreadsheet builds the formula structure for you. MPS is the spreadsheet.

This has a profound consequence: there is no copy-paste from an external text editor into MPS’s TextGen buffers. Building a template character by character through MPS’s completion menus is the default path — and the walled garden problem this creates is addressed in [the-pipeline].

The Entity Concept

An Entity in the DSL represents a domain object — not a database table, not a Go struct, but a business concept with operations and behavior attached.

Entity: User
  fields:
    id        uuid       primaryKey, auto
    username  string     required
    email     email      required     (implies UNIQUE in SQL)
    password  password   hidden       (excluded from JSON responses)
    created_at time      auto
    updated_at time      auto
  operations: create, get, update, delete, list
  hooks on create:
    preCreateD  (pre-sync, priority 1)
    preCreateM  (pre-async, priority 2)
    postCreateNotifyAdmin (post-async, priority 1)

From this declaration, TextGen produces:

// User struct (from field declarations)
type User struct {
    Id        string `json:"id" db:"id"`
    UserName  string `json:"user_name" db:"user_name"`
    UserMail  string `json:"user_mail" db:"user_mail"`
    // Password has no json tag — the "hidden" annotation removes it
    Password  string `db:"password"`
    CreatedAt string `json:"created_at" db:"created_at"`
    UpdatedAt string `json:"updated_at" db:"updated_at"`
}

// Event types (one per operation)
type UserCreatedEvent struct { ... }
type UserGetRequest   struct { ... }
type UserUpdatedEvent struct { ... }
type UserDeletedEvent struct { ... }
type UserListRequest  struct { ... }

// Handler struct
type UserHandler struct {
    natsConn  core.Connection
    publisher core.Publisher
    tracer    tracer.Tracer
    logger    logger.Logger
    // workerpool included only if any hook is async
    wp        *workerpool.WorkerPool
}

// Five Handle methods follow...

The DSL’s field types carry domain semantics that plain Go types do not:

DSL Type Go/SQL equivalent What it implies

uuid

string / UUID

Auto-generated via gen_random_uuid(), primary key candidate

email

string / VARCHAR(255)

UNIQUE constraint in SQL, validation hook target

password

string

hidden annotation: excluded from JSON, policy checking target

time

string / TIMESTAMPTZ

auto means DEFAULT NOW() in SQL

json

string / JSONB

PostgreSQL JSONB storage

entityRef

string / UUID REFERENCES

Foreign key; DAL handles the join

This represents the evolution from SQL-primitive types (int64, string, float) to domain types. With primitive types, email is just string — the developer is responsible for adding the UNIQUE constraint and writing validation separately. With domain types, email is the constraint.

The Relation Concept

A Relation connects two entities with a named set of operations: assign, remove, and list.

Relation: UserRoles
  from: User
  to:   Roles
  operations: assign, remove, list
  extraFields:
    assigned_at  time  auto

From this, TextGen produces:

  • Three event types: UserRolesAssignedEvent, UserRolesRemovedEvent, UserRolesListRequest

  • Three handler methods inside user.go: HandleAssign, HandleRemove, HandleList (for the relation)

  • A junction table in SQL: iam.user_roles with composite primary key and cascade deletes

Relations are generated into the same file as their owning entity (UserRoles → inside user.go, RolesPermissions → inside roles.go). This is a consequence of MPS’s one-concept-one-file constraint. See [the-pipeline] for the full story.

The Hook Concept

A Hook is a named extension point attached to a specific operation. The 2×2 matrix of hook variants:

Pre-operation Post-operation

Sync (blocks, can abort)

func (s *Handler) hookName(ctx, span, event) error

func (s *Handler) hookName(ctx, span, event, data []byte) []byte

Async (fire-and-forget)

func (s *Handler) hookName(ctx, span, event)

func (s *Handler) hookName(ctx, span, event, data []byte)

The four signatures exist because there are four distinct use cases:

  • Pre-sync: Validation and authorization. Returns an error to abort the operation before it reaches the DAL.

  • Pre-async: Audit logging, notifications. Fires without blocking — the operation continues whether or not the async work completes.

  • Post-sync: Data transformation and PII filtering. Receives the DAL response as []byte, returns the modified response.

  • Post-async: Cache invalidation, admin alerts. Fires after the DAL response without blocking the reply to the caller.

Design rationale: The four signatures emerged from customer extensibility requirements. Customers need async audit trails (pre-async) and sync validation (pre-sync) on the same operation. A single hook(ctx, event) ([]byte, error) signature cannot express both — you cannot make a function both blocking-returnable and fire-and-forget simultaneously. The 2×2 separation is intentional: each axis (pre/post, sync/async) is an independent orthogonal choice.

Hook priority controls execution order within a phase. Lower priority number runs first within a phase:

hooks on get:
  filterPII        post-sync   priority 3
  cacheResult      post-sync   priority 2
  enrichData       post-sync   priority 1

Hooks execute in order: enrichData (1) → cacheResult (2) → filterPII (3).

Critical ordering rule: Always place sync validator hooks at a lower priority number (runs first) than async hooks on the same operation. Async hooks are fire-and-forget — if a sync validator fires after an async hook, the async hook has already started even if the sync validator will eventually abort the operation. The async hook keeps running. It cannot be cancelled.

TextGen: The Recipe Book

TextGen is the MPS mechanism for describing code generation templates. Think of it as a smart template engine with type checking.

A TextGen component declares: "for every instance of concept Entity in the sandbox, generate one .go file at path /src/{entity.name.toLowerCase()}.go containing the following content."

The "following content" is expressed as a sequence of append statements:

text gen component for concept Entity {
  file path: "/src/"
  extension: "go"
  file name: node.name.toLowerCase()

  body:
    append {package main\n} ;
    append {\nimport (\n} ;
    append {    "context"\n} ;
    // ... conditional imports based on entity properties ...
    foreach operation in node.operations {
      append {\nfunc (s *} ;
      append ${node.name} ;
      append {Handler) Handle} ;
      append ${operation.name.capitalize()} ;
      append {(msg micro.Request) {\n} ;
      // ... eight-step handler body ...
    }
}

Each append {…​} statement was typed character-by-character in MPS’s projectional editor (before parse_textgen.py existed). The Entity TextGen template is approximately 300 append statements producing ~400 lines of Go per entity.

The template supports conditional logic:

// Only import workerpool if any hook is async
append ${node.needWorkerPool() ? "\"...workerpool\"" : ""} \n ;

// Only validate non-auto, non-hidden, non-nullable fields
foreach field in node.fields {
  if (!(field.hasAnnotation("primaryKey")) && !(field.hasAnnotation("auto"))
      && !(field.hasAnnotation("hidden")) && !(field.hasAnnotation("nullable"))) {
    append {|| event.} ;
    append ${field.name.capitalize()} ;
    append { == ""} ;
  }
}

This is why password fields are excluded from validation (they are hidden) and id fields are excluded (they are primaryKey and auto). The template knows which fields to skip because the DSL field annotations carry that information.

From DSL Declaration to Running Code

The full chain for a single entity:

  1. Developer defines User in MPS with fields, operations, and hooks.

  2. TextGen runs, producing user.go (595 lines) and sqlPrem_init_sql.sql (partial).

  3. sync.sh copies user.go to src/.

  4. merge_hooks.py extracts hook stubs from user.go into userDefinedHooks.go.

  5. Developer implements business logic in userDefinedHooks.go.

  6. sync.sh rebuilds the Docker container.

  7. demo.sh verifies the handler works end-to-end.

Adding a field to User in MPS restarts at step 2. userDefinedHooks.go is preserved at step 4 — the developer’s implementations are not overwritten.

Watch for:

  • Typos in DSL field names propagate faithfully to generated Go struct fields and NATS subject strings. motadata.usr.create (missing 'e') will be silently generated if the entity is named Usr.

  • DSL constraints are not automatically inferred. If a field should be unique, it must be declared as email type (which implies unique) or given an explicit unique annotation. The generator trusts the declaration.

  • The Holder Concept Pattern — an artifact of incomplete MPS editor styling knowledge — adds unnecessary nesting in some entity definitions. If you see a HooksHolder wrapper concept between Entity and Hook, it is a workaround, not a feature. Direct 0..n children with visibility queries would be cleaner.

The Pipeline

The pipeline is the machinery between a DSL declaration and a running Docker container. It is not one script — it is a chain of tools, each solving a problem the previous tool could not.

Understanding the chain requires understanding why each tool exists, which means understanding the constraints that made the naive approach fail.

The Walled Garden

The central constraint of the entire pipeline is MPS’s projectional editor.

In a text editor, templates are text files. They can be written in any editor, AI-assisted, copy-pasted from working code, and versioned as plain text in git.

In MPS, templates are stored as binary .mps XML files. They are authored through MPS’s completion menus — not by typing text, but by selecting nodes and invoking editor actions. There is no way to paste a Go handler from an external editor into a TextGen buffer. There is no way to copy TextGen content out to a plain text file. There is no way to use an AI assistant to help write the template.

This is the walled garden. Everything inside MPS is inaccessible to external tooling. Everything external to MPS cannot enter.

Three walls:

  1. No import: Cannot paste code snippets into TextGen buffers. Every character must be typed through MPS completion menus.

  2. No export: Cannot copy TextGen content to an external file for editing or AI assistance.

  3. No tooling: Cannot use scripts, AI, or any external tool to modify templates directly.

For a 300-append-statement template producing 400 lines of Go per entity, the walled garden means weeks of manual authoring.

The Wrong Escape Route: Find a Better Plugin

The first attempt to escape the walled garden was to switch from native MPS TextGen to the DSL Foundry TextGen plugin.

The attempt failed. Documentation was sparse. The groupings model — how DSL Foundry structures template output — was opaque without guides. After significant time invested, the attempt was abandoned without producing a working template.

The lesson: switching plugins is not always the right escape route. Sometimes the right answer is to build a bridge.

The Right Solution: parse_textgen.py

parse_textgen.py is a Python script that reverse-engineers the MPS TextGen XML format.

The approach:

  1. Examine existing TextGen .mps files from templates that already work.

  2. Map each TextGen node type to its XML representation.

  3. Build a parser that accepts human-readable markdown files that look like TextGen templates.

  4. Convert the markdown to valid .mps XML.

  5. Load the .mps file into MPS as if it were authored natively.

# What you write (plain markdown):
package ${node.name.toLowerCase()}\n

import (\n
    ${node.needWorkerPool() ? '"workerpool"' : ''}\n
)\n

# What parse_textgen.py produces (MPS XML, abbreviated):
<node concept="AppendOperation">
  <property role="text" value="package "/>
  <node concept="NodeReference">
    <ref role="node" to="..."/>
    <node concept="GetProperty">
      <property role="method" value="toLowerCase"/>
    </node>
  </node>
  <property role="text" value="\n"/>
</node>

The reverse engineering consumed one full day including bug fixing. The hardest part: each TextGen node type has a different child arrangement in the XML. String interpolations (${…​}) have a different structure than literal text. Conditional expressions have a different structure than loops. Each combination required its own mapping rule.

The payoff: writing a new TextGen template becomes a matter of authoring a plain markdown file. AI assistance, copy-paste from working Go code, external editors — all become available again. TextGen changes are also diffable in git: markdown diffs instead of binary .mps diffs.

Design rationale: parse_textgen.py is a bridge, not a replacement. MPS still runs TextGen — it reads the .mps file and executes generation as normal. The bridge only changes how templates are authored.

The One-Concept-One-File Constraint

MPS imposes: one root concept instance in the sandbox produces one output file from TextGen.

This constraint reveals itself when separate files are required.

The Wrong Model: Single-File Everything

The natural instinct — especially coming from Prisma — is to define all entities in one place:

Models {
  Entity: User { ... }
  Entity: Roles { ... }
  Entity: Permissions { ... }
}

With MPS TextGen, this produces one file containing all three entity handlers combined. UMAN made this mistake — its TextGen file grew to 560 KB, the largest of all projects. pcrd made the same mistake: it generated working end-to-end code (Go Gin server, SQL schema, Docker setup) but all entities landed in one giant file.

The Right Model: Separate Root Concepts

To get user.go, roles.go, and permissions.go as separate files, each entity must be a separate root concept in the MPS sandbox:

Sandbox:
  Main         (root) → main.go
  User         (root) → user.go   (includes UserRoles relation handlers)
  Roles        (root) → roles.go  (includes RolesPermissions relation handlers)
  Permissions  (root) → permissions.go
  SqlSchem     (root) → sqlPrem_init_sql.sql

Each root concept = one TextGen execution = one output file.

Relations are children of their owning entity, not standalone root concepts. UserRoles lives inside User and generates into user.go. This is why relation handlers appear in the same file as entity handlers — not by coincidence, but by constraint.

Design rationale: The Main concept does not contain entities — it references them via EntityRef nodes. This keeps entity definitions self-contained while allowing main.go to know which handlers to wire up.

Stage 1: MPS TextGen Output

When MPS runs TextGen on the sandbox, it produces raw Go files with #HOOKS_START / #HOOKS_END markers embedded:

// user.go (generated — DO NOT EDIT)

// ... UserHandler struct, constructor, Handle methods ...

// #HOOKS_START
func (s *UserHandler) preCreateD(ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span,
    event *UserCreatedEvent) error {
    return nil
}

func (s *UserHandler) preCreateM(ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span,
    event *UserCreatedEvent) {
}

func (s *UserHandler) postCreateNotifyAdmin(ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span,
    event *UserCreatedEvent, data []byte) {
}
// #HOOKS_END

The markers exist because userDefinedHooks.go must be a separate file — but MPS cannot generate it directly without creating a cluttering root concept. The solution: generate stubs inside entity files, then extract them externally.

Stage 2: merge_hooks.py — Hook Extraction and Merge

merge_hooks.py reads every generated entity file, extracts the stubs between #HOOKS_START and #HOOKS_END, and merges them into userDefinedHooks.go.

The merge has three outcomes per hook stub:

Outcome Condition

Add

Hook stub is new — not yet in userDefinedHooks.go. Appended.

Skip

Hook stub already exists in userDefinedHooks.go with matching signature. Developer’s implementation is preserved.

Replace

Hook stub exists but signature has changed (sync ↔ async flip). Stub is replaced; old implementation is printed as a warning.

Identity key: *ReceiverType.funcName (e.g., *UserHandler.preCreateD). This prevents collisions when multiple entity handlers have hooks with the same name — *UserHandler.preCreate and *RolesHandler.preCreate are distinct keys.

War Story: The Signature Mismatch

A hook was changed from post-sync to post-async. The signature changed from:

// Before: post-sync — transforms response, returns []byte
func (s *UserHandler) postCreate(ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span,
    event *UserCreatedEvent, data []byte) []byte {
    // developer's implementation
    return modifiedData
}

to:

// After: post-async — fire-and-forget, no return value
func (s *UserHandler) postCreate(ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span,
    event *UserCreatedEvent, data []byte) {
}

The name stayed the same. Before signature change detection was added, merge_hooks.py kept the old implementation — with the wrong return type. The build broke with a type error.

The fix: compare signatures on every merge, not just names. When a mismatch is detected, the old implementation is printed to stdout as a warning and the stub is replaced. The developer sees the warning and migrates the logic manually.

Principle: Presence is not equivalence. A function with the right name and the wrong shape is not the right function.

Stage 3: sync.sh — Copy, Merge, Patch, Build

sync.sh orchestrates the full pipeline in eight steps:

# Step 1: Copy .go and .sql from MPS source_gen/ into src/
cp source_gen/*.go src/
cp source_gen/*.sql src/

# Step 2: Run merge_hooks.py
python3 merge_hooks.py

# Step 3: Extract project name from main.go first-line comment
APP_NAME=$(head -1 src/main.go | sed 's|^// *||')

# Step 4: Sync vendored SDK
rsync -av ~/projects/nextgen/gosdk/motadata-go-sdk/ motadata-go-sdk/

# Step 5: Patch SDK module path (motadatagosdk → dev.azure.com/...)
sed -i 's|^module motadatagosdk|module dev.azure.com/Motadata/NextGen/motadata-go-sdk|' \
    motadata-go-sdk/go.mod

# Step 6: Fix SDK internal imports
find motadata-go-sdk -name '*.go' -exec sed -i \
    's|"motadatagosdk/|"dev.azure.com/Motadata/NextGen/motadata-go-sdk/|g' {} +

# Step 7: Kill lingering processes on service ports
fuser -k 4229/tcp 8222/tcp 2>/dev/null || true

# Step 8: Build and start Docker Compose
docker compose build --build-arg APP_NAME="$APP_NAME"
docker compose up -d

The SDK Module Path Problem

The Motadata Go SDK is vendored — copied locally — because it is not published to a Go module registry.

The SDK source uses motadatagosdk as its module name. The generated Go files import dev.azure.com/Motadata/NextGen/motadata-go-sdk/events/core. These do not match — Go refuses to build.

sync.sh patches the mismatch in steps 5 and 6. The sed commands are idempotent: patching an already-patched file is safe, so every sync.sh run leaves the SDK in a consistent state.

When the SDK is eventually published to a registry, steps 4–6 can be removed entirely. The generated imports will resolve directly via go mod.

Design rationale: The project name flows from DSL → generated comment → sync.sh extraction → Docker build arg → container name. A config file would be cleaner, but the first-line comment is generated automatically from the DSL’s NatsServer concept. Single source of truth: change the name in MPS and it propagates through the entire stack.

Stage 4: Docker Compose

Two services in docker-compose.yml:

  • nats: nats:2.10-alpine with JetStream enabled, healthcheck on :8222/healthz

  • app: Built from Dockerfile, waits for NATS to be healthy before starting

Port mapping: * 4229:4222 — NATS client port (external 4229, internal 4222) * 8222:8222 — NATS HTTP monitoring

The port mismatch (4229 vs 4222) exists because 4222 was already in use on the development machine. It is a local conflict resolution, not an architectural choice.

The app connects to nats://nats:4222 on the internal Docker network. demo.sh connects to nats://localhost:4229 from the host.

Step 7 in sync.sh (fuser -k 4229/tcp 8222/tcp) clears any lingering processes before each rebuild, preventing port conflicts from previous runs.

The Full Pipeline in One View

MPS DSL (UserManagmentMps/)
  │
  │  Author TextGen templates via markdown + parse_textgen.py
  │  (escapes walled garden)
  │
  ▼
TextGen generates:
  source_gen/main.go          155 lines
  source_gen/user.go          595 lines + #HOOKS markers
  source_gen/roles.go         481 lines + #HOOKS markers
  source_gen/permissions.go   307 lines + #HOOKS markers
  source_gen/sqlPrem_init_sql.sql  31 lines
  │
  │  sync.sh step 1: copy to src/
  │
  ▼
src/*.go  (copied, will be overwritten on next sync)
  │
  │  sync.sh step 2: merge_hooks.py
  │    - extract stubs from #HOOKS markers
  │    - add new / skip existing / replace changed-signature
  │
  ▼
src/userDefinedHooks.go  221 lines, 30+ stubs, preserved across regeneration
  │
  │  sync.sh steps 3–6: name extraction, SDK rsync + patch
  │
  ▼
motadata-go-sdk/  vendored, module path patched to dev.azure.com/...
  │
  │  sync.sh steps 7–8: kill old processes, docker compose build + up
  │
  ▼
Running container on port 4229 (NATS microservice)
  │
  │  demo.sh: 21 e2e tests with mock DAL
  │
  ▼
All 21 tests pass ✓

Watch for:

  • Running sync.sh without MPS having regenerated first. The script copies from source_gen/ — if those files are stale, the container is stale.

  • Manually editing files in src/ other than userDefinedHooks.go. Overwritten at step 1.

  • Hook signature changes that go unnoticed. merge_hooks.py prints a warning but does not fail the build. Check stdout after every sync that modifies a hook definition in MPS.

  • The user_roless double-s bug: junction table iam.user_roless has a doubled suffix because a hardcoded "s" string was appended to entity names that already ended in s. Always use DSL variables for name construction, not hardcoded string fragments.

The Developer Flow

This section traces the complete workflow for adding a new entity to the system. The example is the Permissions entity — the third entity added after User and Roles were already working.

The six steps:

  1. Define the entity in MPS (fields, operations)

  2. Define hooks on operations

  3. Define relations (RolesPermissions)

  4. Run TextGen to generate Go files

  5. Run sync.sh to copy, merge, patch, and rebuild

  6. Run demo.sh to verify

Step 1: Define the Entity in MPS

Open MPS, navigate to the UserManagmentMps project, and create a new root node of type Entity.

The projectional editor presents a structured form — not a text file. Fill in the entity name, then add fields one by one using completion menus.

Entity: Permissions
  fields:
    id          uuid     primaryKey, auto
    name        string   required
    description text     nullable
    created_at  time     auto
  operations: create, get, update, delete, list

The DSL editor validates as you type. uuid + primaryKey tells the generator to produce UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() in SQL. text + nullable tells it to omit NOT NULL. time + auto produces TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW().

Compare this to the User entity:

Entity: User
  fields:
    id          uuid     primaryKey, auto
    username    string   required
    email       email    required
    password    password hidden
    created_at  time     auto
    updated_at  time     auto
  operations: create, get, update, delete, list

The structure is identical — same field type vocabulary, same operation list, same annotation system. The generator sees the same pattern and applies the same template. The output will be a permissions.go file with the same eight-step structure as user.go and roles.go, with Permissions-specific type names and subjects.

The faithful propagation rule: Typos in DSL field names propagate without correction. If the entity is named Permissons (missing an 'i'), the generated file will be permissons.go, the NATS subject will be motadata.permissons.create, and the SQL table will be iam.permissons. The generator trusts the declaration. MPS constraints can catch some errors (duplicate names, missing required fields) but cannot catch semantic mistakes like misspellings.

Step 2: Define Hooks

With the entity defined, add hooks to specific operations. In MPS, hooks are children of an operation within the entity definition.

Entity: Permissions
  ...
  hooks on create:
    preCreateValidate  (pre-sync,  priority 1)   ← blocks; can abort
    preCreateAudit     (pre-async, priority 2)   ← fire-and-forget logging
    postCreateNotify   (post-async, priority 1)  ← fire-and-forget alert

When a hook is added, the generator:

  1. Includes the hook stub in the generated permissions.go between #HOOKS_START and #HOOKS_END markers.

  2. Includes the hook call in the HandleCreate method at the correct phase (pre-hooks before DAL forward, post-hooks after).

  3. Sorts hooks by priority within each phase before generating the dispatch code.

Priority and async interaction: preCreateValidate runs first (priority 1, sync). It can return an error to abort the operation before the DAL is called. preCreateAudit runs second (priority 2, async) — it has already been dispatched to the workerpool by the time the main goroutine continues. If preCreateValidate fails on a later request, preCreateAudit will have already fired for that request. Place sync validators at lower priority numbers than async hooks to ensure validation runs before async work begins.

The conditional import logic is worth noting here. Because preCreateAudit and postCreateNotify are async, the TextGen template detects that the entity needWorkerPool() and includes the workerpool import in the generated file. If all hooks were sync, the workerpool import would be omitted entirely.

Step 3: Define Relations

A relation connecting Roles to Permissions is a separate concept in MPS, defined as a child of the Roles entity:

Entity: Roles
  ...
  Relation: RolesPermissions
    from: Roles
    to:   Permissions
    operations: assign, remove, list
    extraFields:
      granted_at  time  auto

Compare to UserRoles:

Entity: User
  ...
  Relation: UserRoles
    from: User
    to:   Roles
    operations: assign, remove, list
    extraFields:
      assigned_at  time  auto

The template is identical — only the entity names and field names differ. RolesPermissions generates into roles.go (because it is a child of Roles). UserRoles generates into user.go (because it is a child of User).

This gives three handler methods inside roles.go:

func (s *RolesHandler) HandleAssign(msg micro.Request)  { ... }
func (s *RolesHandler) HandleRemove(msg micro.Request)  { ... }
func (s *RolesHandler) HandleList(msg micro.Request)    { ... }

With NATS subjects:

  • motadata.roles.permissions.assign

  • motadata.roles.permissions.remove

  • motadata.roles.permissions.list

Step 4: Run TextGen

In MPS, right-click the root node → "Preview Generated Text" to see what will be produced. This is the fastest feedback loop — it shows the output inline without file I/O, without running sync.sh, without rebuilding Docker.

Use "Preview Generated Text" to verify:

  • The struct fields match the declaration (correct types, correct annotations)

  • The operation methods are present (HandleCreate, HandleGet, etc.)

  • The hook calls appear in the correct phase order

  • The #HOOKS_START / #HOOKS_END markers are present with the correct stub signatures

When the preview looks correct, trigger full TextGen (right-click → "Generate Text") to write the files to source_gen/.

MPS generates: * source_gen/permissions.go — Permissions entity handler (~307 lines) * Updated source_gen/roles.go — now includes RolesPermissions relation handlers * Updated source_gen/sqlPrem_init_sql.sql — now includes iam.permissions table (if SqlSchem references the new entity)

The SqlSchem reference gap: The SQL schema only generates tables for entities that are referenced in the SqlSchem root concept’s entityrefs list. Adding Permissions as an entity does not automatically add it to the SQL schema. A reference to Permissions in the SqlSchem root must also be added. This was the cause of the missing Permissions table in the initial deployment — the entity existed, the handler worked, but the table was never created.

Step 5: Run sync.sh

sync.sh is the transition from "files on disk" to "running service." It is also the step with the most ways to go wrong.

./sync.sh

What happens, in order:

  1. permissions.go is copied from source_gen/ to src/. Previous src/permissions.go (if any) is overwritten.

  2. merge_hooks.py runs. It finds #HOOKS_START in src/permissions.go and extracts three new stubs: preCreateValidate, preCreateAudit, postCreateNotify. These are appended to userDefinedHooks.go.

  3. roles.go is also copied and merged — the RolesPermissions hooks appear as new stubs.

  4. SDK is rsynced and patched.

  5. Docker container is rebuilt and restarted.

After sync.sh, open userDefinedHooks.go:

// New stubs appended by merge_hooks.py:

func (s *PermissionsHandler) preCreateValidate(
    ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span, event *PermissionsCreatedEvent) error {
    return nil
}

func (s *PermissionsHandler) preCreateAudit(
    ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span, event *PermissionsCreatedEvent) {
}

func (s *PermissionsHandler) postCreateNotify(
    ctx context.Context, span tracer.Span, event *PermissionsCreatedEvent, data []byte) {
}

The stubs are empty. Implement the business logic here. On the next sync.sh run, merge_hooks.py will skip these stubs (they already exist with matching signatures) and preserve the implementations.

War Story: The Trailing Dot Bug

During early development of the Permissions entity, a generated handler contained:

if event.Permissions. == "" {
    // validation
}

A trailing dot — event.Permissions. — with nothing after it. The Go compiler caught this immediately, but the root cause was not obvious.

Tracing backward: the TextGen template iterates node.fields and for each non-auto, non-hidden, non-nullable field, appends:

append {|| event.} ;
append ${field.name.capitalize()} ;
append { == ""} ;

field.name.capitalize() returned an empty string. The field in MPS had been created in the editor but not named. The MPS editor allows a field to exist with an empty name — there is no constraint preventing it.

TextGen generated event. + "" + ` == ""` = event. == "".

The fix: give the field a name, or delete it.

Principle: Silent generation failures produce syntactically invalid code. The symptom appears in the compiler, not in MPS. When a Go compile error looks like a template expansion artifact (trailing dots, empty identifiers, doubled strings), trace backward to the TextGen node that produced that line — not to the Go code itself.

Step 6: Run demo.sh

./demo.sh

demo.sh connects to nats://localhost:4229 and runs 21 tests. For the Permissions entity, it spawns a mock DAL responder:

nats reply "motadata.permissions.db.>" '{"status":"ok"}' &

Then sends test messages:

# Test: valid permission create
nats req motadata.permissions.create \
    '{"name":"read:users","description":"Can read user list"}'

# Test: missing required field (name)
nats req motadata.permissions.create \
    '{"description":"No name provided"}'

# Expected: validation error response

A passing test suite confirms:

  • The NATS subjects are correctly registered (service discovery works)

  • Validation fires on missing required fields

  • Pre-hooks run in priority order

  • DAL forwarding works (mock responder replies, main handler returns the reply)

  • Post-hooks fire

What Can Go Wrong at Each Step

Step Symptom Root Cause

Define entity

Wrong field type in generated struct

Field declared with wrong DSL type; generator trusts the declaration

Define entity

Missing SQL table

Entity not referenced in SqlSchem root’s entityrefs list

Define hooks

Async hook fires even when sync validator aborts

Async hook has lower priority number than sync validator — runs first

Run TextGen

Trailing dot in generated code

Field in MPS editor has empty name string

Run TextGen

user_roless double suffix in SQL

Hardcoded "s" suffix appended to entity name that already ends in 's'

Run sync.sh

Old hook implementation broken after sync

Hook changed from sync to async (signature mismatch); check merge_hooks.py stdout for warning

Run sync.sh

Build fails: cannot find module

SDK rsync didn’t complete or module path patch failed; check motadata-go-sdk/go.mod

Run demo.sh

Test times out instead of failing

No mock DAL responder for the new entity’s .db. subjects; add nats reply for the entity

Watch for:

  • Running demo.sh before sync.sh completes. Docker Compose takes time to become healthy — demo.sh connects immediately and may see the old container.

  • Implementing hook logic that depends on DAL response format before verifying the mock DAL response matches production DAL format. Mock responders return {"status":"ok"} for everything — production DAL returns entity-specific JSON.

  • Forgetting that hook implementations in userDefinedHooks.go are not regenerated. If a hook is renamed in MPS, the old implementation remains in userDefinedHooks.go under the old name, unused. The new stub is appended with an empty body. The old implementation must be manually migrated and deleted.

The User Flow

A request enters the system as a NATS message. It exits as a NATS reply. Everything in between — unmarshaling, pre-hooks, validation, DAL forwarding, post-hooks — happens inside the UserManagement service in a single synchronous chain per handler method.

This section traces that chain from the caller’s perspective.

The Subject Hierarchy

The service registers endpoints on a tree of NATS subjects. Every subject follows the pattern motadata.{entity}.{operation}.

The full set of registered subjects for the three entities and two relations:

# Entity operations (15 total)
motadata.user.create
motadata.user.get
motadata.user.update
motadata.user.delete
motadata.user.list

motadata.roles.create
motadata.roles.get
motadata.roles.update
motadata.roles.delete
motadata.roles.list

motadata.permissions.create
motadata.permissions.get
motadata.permissions.update
motadata.permissions.delete
motadata.permissions.list

# Relation operations (6 total)
motadata.user.roles.assign
motadata.user.roles.remove
motadata.user.roles.list

motadata.roles.permissions.assign
motadata.roles.permissions.remove
motadata.roles.permissions.list

Twenty-one registered endpoints. Each maps to one handler method in the generated Go code.

The DAL subjects follow the same pattern with .db. inserted:

motadata.user.create         →  motadata.user.db.create
motadata.roles.list          →  motadata.roles.db.list
motadata.user.roles.assign   →  motadata.user.roles.db.assign

The service is transparent in both directions: callers use the business subjects, the DAL uses the db subjects, and the service bridges them.

Tracing One Request End-to-End

Scenario: a caller creates a new user.

nats req motadata.user.create \
    '{"username":"alice","user_mail":"alice@example.com","password":"s3cr3t"}'

Step 1: NATS delivers the message. The NATS micro service routes the message to UserHandler.HandleCreate based on the registered subject.

Step 2: OTEL span starts.

ctx, span := s.tracer.Start(ctx, "user.create")
defer span.End()

Everything from this point happens within the span.

Step 3: Unmarshal.

var event UserCreatedEvent
if err := json.Unmarshal(msg.Data(), &event); err != nil {
    msg.Error("400", "invalid JSON", nil)
    return
}

If the body is not valid JSON, the handler replies immediately with a 400 error. No hooks run.

Step 4: Pre-hooks run in priority order.

// Pre-sync hook (priority 1) — can abort
if err := s.preCreateD(ctx, span, &event); err != nil {
    msg.Error("422", err.Error(), nil)
    return
}

// Pre-async hook (priority 2) — fire-and-forget
_ = workerpool.AsyncWithCtx(ctx, s.wp, func() {
    s.preCreateM(ctx, span, &event)
})

The sync hook runs first. If it returns an error, the handler aborts — the async hook has not been dispatched yet and does not run. The async hook fires after the sync hook passes, dispatched to the workerpool; the main goroutine continues immediately.

Step 5: Validate required fields.

if event.UserName == "" || event.UserMail == "" {
    msg.Error("400", "missing required fields", nil)
    return
}

Generated validation — TextGen iterates non-auto, non-hidden, non-nullable fields and builds this condition. Password is excluded (it is hidden). ID is excluded (it is primaryKey and auto).

Step 6: Set span attributes.

span.SetAttributes(
    attribute.String("user.username", event.UserName),
    attribute.String("user.email", event.UserMail),
)

Step 7: Forward to DAL.

dalResp, err := s.publisher.Request(
    ctx,
    "motadata.user.db.create",
    requestBody,
    headers,
    30*time.Second,
)
if err != nil {
    msg.Error("503", "DAL timeout", nil)
    return
}

Synchronous NATS request-reply with a 30-second timeout. The handler blocks until the DAL responds or the timeout fires.

Step 8: Post-hooks run.

// Post-sync hook — transforms response
responseData = s.postGetFilterPII(ctx, span, &event, dalResp.Data())

// Post-async hook — fire-and-forget
_ = workerpool.AsyncWithCtx(ctx, s.wp, func() {
    s.postCreateNotifyAdmin(ctx, span, &event, responseData)
})

Post-sync hooks receive the DAL response as []byte and return the (possibly modified) []byte. Post-async hooks receive the response data but their return value is discarded.

Step 9: Reply to caller.

msg.Respond(responseData)

The caller receives the DAL’s response, possibly transformed by post-sync hooks.

Hook Execution Model

Pre-operation Post-operation

Sync

Runs in-line. Returns error to abort. Caller waits.

Runs in-line. Receives []byte, returns modified []byte. Caller waits.

Async

Dispatched to workerpool. Returns nothing. Caller does not wait.

Dispatched to workerpool. Receives []byte read-only. Caller does not wait.

Practical implications:

  • Validation belongs in pre-sync. Only pre-sync hooks can prevent the operation from reaching the DAL.

  • Audit logging belongs in pre-async or post-async. It should not block the operation.

  • PII filtering belongs in post-sync. It transforms the response before the caller sees it.

  • Cache invalidation belongs in post-async. It runs after the caller receives the response.

Async hook error handling: The line _ = workerpool.AsyncWithCtx(…​) discards the workerpool’s return value. Errors inside async hooks are swallowed — they do not propagate to the caller and do not abort the operation. This is intentional: fire-and-forget means the caller’s flow is decoupled from the hook’s outcome. If an async hook must report errors, it must do so internally (log, metric, alert) — not by returning an error.

Service Discovery

The NATS micro protocol provides built-in service discovery:

nats req '$SRV.INFO' ''

The response includes the service name, version, and the full list of registered endpoints. Test #21 in demo.sh verifies this — service discoverability is the final check after all 20 entity and relation tests pass.

The service name in the response derives from the DSL’s NatsServer concept → first-line comment in main.go → sync.sh extraction → Docker build argument. One declaration in MPS populates the discovery response.

Error Patterns

Three categories of errors:

Error Caller Response Root Cause

Invalid JSON

400 invalid JSON immediately

json.Unmarshal fails; no hooks run

Validation failure

400 missing required fields or hook-specific error

Required field empty, or pre-sync hook returns error

DAL timeout

503 DAL timeout after 30 seconds

DAL did not respond within the timeout window

There is no retry logic. A DAL timeout means the caller receives a 503 and must decide whether to retry. The service does not retry on the caller’s behalf.

Watch for:

  • Pre-async hooks that fire before pre-sync validation. If the async hook starts an irreversible action (sending an email, writing an audit record) and the sync validator then aborts the operation, the irreversible action has already happened. Priority ordering is the only protection — place sync validators at lower priority numbers (runs first).

  • Post-sync hooks that panic. A panic in a post-sync hook crashes the request goroutine; the caller never receives a response and the connection times out rather than getting a clean error.

  • Long-running pre-sync hooks. Because they block the request path, a slow pre-sync hook directly increases response latency for every caller. Use pre-async for anything that might take more than a few milliseconds.

Lessons and Red Flags

Every system reveals failure modes after it is built. This section documents the ones this system revealed — as specific incidents with forensics and named signals.

Each follows the same four-part structure:

  1. Incident — what went wrong, exactly

  2. Forensics — how the root cause was found

  3. Principle — the generalizable rule

  4. Signal — how to recognize the pattern before it breaks

Lesson 1: The Single-File Trap

Incident

UMAN generated working Go code. The code compiled, the tests passed (such as they were), and the Prisma-style schema definition felt natural. But all entities and their handlers were in a single generated file.

When a fourth entity was added, the single file grew past 1,000 lines. When a template bug was found, fixing it required mentally tracking which section of the 1,000-line file corresponded to which entity.

The project was abandoned — not because generation failed, but because the output structure was unmaintainable.

Forensics

The root cause was the MPS one-concept-one-file constraint, but the trigger was choosing a Prisma-style single-model definition. Prisma works because it generates a single schema file and all code is human-readable and separate. MPS TextGen puts all output from a single root concept into one file — the organizational discipline of Prisma (one schema, many generated files) does not translate.

The same mistake appeared in pcrd: entity/relation declarations, Go Gin server, SQL schema, Docker setup — all generated and working, all in one file. Two working systems, both abandoned for the same structural reason.

Principle

The generated output structure mirrors the DSL model structure.

If the DSL model puts everything in one root concept, the generated output is one file. To get N files, N root concepts are required — one per generated output.

This is not a limitation to work around. It is the MPS architecture. Design the DSL model to produce the output structure you want, not the structure that feels natural to declare.

Signal

The trap is active when:

  • The generated file grows proportionally to entity count

  • Searching within a generated file for "the Roles section" becomes necessary

  • Adding a new entity requires scrolling to the right place in the generated output

The fix: split the DSL model into separate root concepts, one per desired output file.

Lesson 2: The Hook Name Collision

Incident

merge_hooks.py keyed hook stubs by function name. When UserRoles and RolesPermissions both had a hook named preAssignHook, the second hook’s stub overwrote the first in userDefinedHooks.go.

The UserRoles implementation was silently replaced with the RolesPermissions stub. The UserRoles assign operation then did nothing — the hook ran but used the empty stub.

Forensics

The merge script compared function names: preAssignHook == preAssignHook. Both hooks had the same name. The merge logic found a "match" and skipped the second stub, which meant the first entity’s implementation was treated as the correct implementation for both.

The receiver type was not part of the identity key: *UserHandler.preAssignHook and *RolesHandler.preAssignHook are different functions, but the script saw them as preAssignHook and preAssignHook — identical.

Principle

Identity requires context.

A function name is not a unique identifier in a codebase with multiple receiver types. preAssignHook on *UserHandler and preAssignHook on *RolesHandler are different functions that happen to share a name. The full identity is ReceiverType.FunctionName.

The fix: key stubs by *ReceiverType.funcName (e.g., *UserHandler.preAssignHook vs. *RolesHandler.preAssignHook).

Signal

The trap is active when:

  • Merge or matching logic uses function names without qualifying the containing type or scope

  • Two different entities have hooks with the same name and different implementations

  • Silently correct-looking output (no error, just wrong behavior) appears after a merge

Lesson 3: Presence Is Not Equivalence

Incident

A hook was changed from post-sync to post-async. The return type changed from []byte to nothing. The name stayed the same.

merge_hooks.py found the hook in userDefinedHooks.go, saw the name matched, and kept the existing implementation — with the old return type.

The Go compiler reported a type error. The error message pointed to the hook implementation in userDefinedHooks.go, not to the merge script that caused the problem.

Forensics

The merge script checked: "does this function name already exist in userDefinedHooks.go?" It did. The script concluded: "this is an existing hook, preserve it."

But "exists" is not the same as "correct shape." The existing function had the wrong signature for the new hook type. The merge script had no concept of signature validation — it only checked for name presence.

Principle

Presence is not equivalence.

Finding a function by name does not mean the function is the right function. A hook with the correct name and the wrong signature is not a match — it is a collision waiting to break the build.

The fix: compare signatures on every merge, not just names. When a signature mismatch is detected, print the old implementation as a warning and replace the stub.

Signal

The trap is active when:

  • Existence checks are the only form of identity validation

  • A script that merges or updates code checks "does it exist?" but not "does it look right?"

  • Build errors appear in preserved user code, not in generated code

Lesson 4: Silent Generation Failures

Incident

A generated handler contained:

if event.Permissions. == "" {

A trailing dot — event.Permissions. — with nothing after it. The Go compiler reported a syntax error. The error pointed to the generated file.

The generated file is not supposed to be edited. When a generated file has a bug, the fix must be in the generator — not in the file itself.

Forensics

TextGen produces this line from:

append {|| event.} ;
append ${field.name.capitalize()} ;
append { == ""} ;

field.name.capitalize() returned an empty string. The field in MPS had been created in the editor but not named. The MPS editor allows a field to exist with an empty name — there is no constraint preventing it.

TextGen generated event. + "" + ` == ""` = event. == "".

Principle

Silent generation failures produce syntactically invalid output.

When TextGen expands a template with an empty or missing value, it produces whatever character combination results from the concatenation. There is no TextGen equivalent of a null check or a "required field" error during generation.

Two protections are available:

  1. Add MPS constraints to the concept (e.g., "name must be non-empty") — the editor will show an error before generation runs.

  2. Add System.out.println(field.name) inside the TextGen template to log intermediate values to the MPS Messages console during generation.

Signal

The trap is active when:

  • A generated Go file has a syntax error that looks like a template artifact (trailing dots, empty identifiers, doubled strings)

  • The error points to a line that no human wrote

  • The instinct is to edit the generated file to fix it

The fix is always in the generator — either the DSL model has a missing value, or the TextGen template is not handling empty values defensively.

Lesson 5: Don’t Fight the Walled Garden — Build a Bridge

Incident

Writing the 300-append-statement Entity TextGen template character by character in MPS’s projectional editor took weeks. Every string interpolation required navigating completion menus. Copy-paste from an external editor was impossible. AI assistance was unavailable. When a bug appeared on line 47 of the generated output, there was no way to set a breakpoint or trace which append statement produced that line.

The first escape attempt — switching to the DSL Foundry TextGen plugin — failed for lack of documentation and incomprehensible groupings.

Forensics

The root cause was accepting the walled garden as a fixed constraint. "This must be typed in MPS" became the unquestioned premise.

The correct question was: "what is MPS actually doing when TextGen runs?" The answer: MPS reads .mps XML files and interprets the TextGen node structure they contain. The .mps format is the real input — the projectional editor is just one way to produce it.

Principle

When a tool’s editing UX is the blocker, build a bridge to it rather than fighting within it.

The walled garden walls are high on the inside. From the outside, the .mps file format is just XML. A Python script can write valid XML. The bridge (parse_textgen.py) took one day to build and eliminated weeks of manual authoring for every future template.

Signal

The trap is active when:

  • Multiple days have been spent manually authoring something that could be expressed in a text file

  • The tool does not allow import from external formats

  • Plugin switching has been tried and failed

The pattern name: reverse-engineer the import format. Find out what the tool actually reads, not what it displays. Build a converter that produces that format from something editable externally.

Lesson 6: External Scripts Are First-Class Tooling

Incident

userDefinedHooks.go needed to exist as a separate file from generated entity handlers. The MPS one-concept-one-file constraint said: to generate a separate file, create a separate root concept. Creating a root concept just for hook stubs would add a trivial one-liner to the sandbox — cluttering it with noise.

The same problem applied to the SQL schema file: the SqlSchem root concept needs explicit entityrefs to include each entity. Forgetting to add a reference means the table is not generated — silently.

Forensics

Both problems share a structure: MPS’s generation model produces files but cannot process or coordinate the output of multiple generation passes. It cannot extract hooks from all entity files and combine them into one file. It cannot verify that all entities have been referenced in SqlSchem.

External scripts have no such limitation.

Principle

External scripts are first-class tooling, not workarounds.

merge_hooks.py is not a hack around MPS’s limitations. It is the right tool for the job MPS cannot do: extract, merge, and validate across multiple generated files. sync.sh is not a workaround for the SDK registry gap — it is the right tool for coordinating the full pipeline.

The pattern: generate inside MPS → transform and coordinate outside MPS.

Signal

The trap is active when:

  • A new MPS root concept is being created just to generate a file that combines or processes output from other concepts

  • A build failure happens because two separately generated files are inconsistent

  • Post-processing logic is being added inside a TextGen template

Principles Reference Card

Name Principle Watch For

The Single-File Trap

Generated output structure mirrors DSL model structure

Generated file growing with entity count; searching within generated output

Identity Requires Context

ReceiverType.FunctionName is the minimum unique identity for a hook

Name-only matching in merge scripts; silent behavior changes after merge

Presence Is Not Equivalence

Name match without signature match is a collision, not a hit

Existence-only checks; build errors in preserved user code

Silent Generation Failures

TextGen produces whatever concatenation results from template + values

Trailing dots, empty identifiers, doubled strings in generated code

Bridge the Walled Garden

Reverse-engineer the tool’s import format; build a converter

Weeks of manual authoring; failed plugin switches; no AI assistance

External Scripts Are First-Class

Generate inside MPS, coordinate outside MPS

New root concepts for post-processing; inconsistency between generated files

Final watch-for:

Scoping in MPS remains partially understood. The current DSL sidesteps complex scoping by using entity references by name rather than variable binding. If future DSL features require computed fields, conditional logic in templates, or cross-entity references at generation time, scoping will need to be properly mastered. The ScopeProvider.getScope() mechanism exists but was not needed for this project — and "did not need it" is not the same as "understood it." Do not assume the scoping knowledge from learning projects (gtog, calculator) is sufficient for production use without verification.
